title: Yesterday
job: Past tense — the first big divergence
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The everyday Italian past is TWO words: a helper plus a participle — ho mangiato. There is no separate one-word past to reach for at this level, and nothing is fronted to make a question or a negative out of it.

The helper splits, and this is the module's one loud thing. Most verbs take avere: ho mangiato, ho bevuto, ho parlato. A short fixed set takes essere — going, coming, staying, being, becoming, and every reflexive verb: sono andato, sono stata. It is a LIST to learn, not a category to derive: camminare ("to walk") is motion and still takes avere.

With essere the participle agrees with the subject, exactly like an adjective: sono andato (a man) · sono andata (a woman) · sono andati (more than one). With avere it never moves at all: ho mangiato, whoever is speaking.

The participle is built from the verb's class: -are gives -ato (parlare → parlato), -ere gives -uto (bere → bevuto), -ire gives -ito (dormire → dormito). Irregular ones exist and are learned one at a time.
non goes in front of the WHOLE verb, helper included: Non ho studiato, never Ho non studiato. English splits its negative around the helper; Italian never splits anything.
ho mangiato translates "I ate" as readily as "I have eaten". One Italian tense covers both English pasts in ordinary speech, so there is no choice to make and no "did" to invent.

Italian has a second past, the imperfetto (mangiavo, ero, avevo), for habits and background. It belongs to a later level; every sentence here is anchored with ieri, so nothing in this module needs it.

words.note: yesterday. It stands at the front or at the end and needs no preposition — the same freedom oggi has.
avere — to have, two jobs. Here it is the helper that builds the past: ho mangiato, hai mangiato, ha mangiato. Alone it is possession, and in M9 hunger and cold: ho fame. The h is silent.
The participle of mangiare — an -are verb, so its ending is -ato. Behind avere it never changes shape, whoever is speaking.

sentences.trap: English has one word for the past — "ate". Italian has two, and both are compulsory: the helper says who, the participle says what.
sentences.sound: YEH-ri: the initial i is a y-glide, so it is two syllables. In ho the h is silent — always, in every Italian word — so it is simply "o".

variations.changed: swap what was eaten — the two-word verb is untouched
ho → hai and a question mark: the helper carries the person, and nothing is fronted

variations.display: Ieri non ho mangiato una pizza
variations.cue: Yesterday I didn't eat a pizza
variations.changed: non in front of the whole verb — it never slips between ho and mangiato

mistake.why: The helper is not optional: ho mangiato. Without it, nothing in the sentence says who ate.

sentences.usage: The first thing anyone is asked about yesterday.
sentences.mnemonic: Two words for one past: who, then what.

words.note: The participle of bere. bere is an -ere verb, so its ending is -uto — and the v of bevo comes back for it: bevuto, not beuto.

sentences.trap: The verb's CLASS decides the participle's ending, and bere is an -ere verb even though its plain form has worn short. That is where -uto comes from.
sentences.sound: be-VU-to, stressed in the middle. All three vowels stay clean and none is swallowed.

variations.display: Ieri ho bevuto un po' di caffè
variations.cue: Yesterday I drank a bit of coffee
variations.changed: the amount phrase slots in where the article was
ho → hai: the helper moves to you, the participle does not
non in front of the whole verb, and no article once the amount is open

mistake.why: bere is an -ere verb, so its participle takes -uto: bevuto.

sentences.usage: Recounting an ordinary day, drink by drink.

words.note: The participle of comprare, "to buy" — an -are verb, so -ato. Buying is done to a thing, so the helper is avere and the participle does not move.

sentences.trap: English fronts "did" to ask or to deny in the past. Italian never adds anything — the helper it already has does both jobs on its own.
sentences.sound: kom-PRA-to. The r is one tap, and the o at the end is short and round.

variations.changed: ho → hai, and a question mark instead of a fronted "did"
swap what was bought — comprato does not agree with it
ho → ha for a third person; the participle still does not move

mistake.why: comprare takes avere: Ieri ho comprato un libro. essere is only for the short going-and-staying list.

sentences.usage: Saying what you did with an afternoon.
sentences.mnemonic: Buying happens to a thing, so it rides avere.

words.note: The participle of lavorare (M4) — an -are verb, so -ato. The stress moves to the -ra- that the ending brings with it.

sentences.trap: English splits its past negative around the helper — did not work. Italian never splits anything: non sits in front of ho, and ho and lavorato stay glued together.
sentences.sound: la-vo-RA-to, four light syllables with the stress on the third, and both r's are single taps.

variations.changed: drop non and the sentence turns positive
swap the time phrase — the negative and the verb are untouched
ho → hai, the time word to the end, and a question mark

mistake.why: non goes in front of the WHOLE verb, helper included: Ieri non ho lavorato.

sentences.mnemonic: non guards the front door, and the two-word verb comes through it together.

words.note: The participle of andare — on the short essere list, so its past is built with sono, never ho: sono andato. With essere the participle agrees: -o a man, -a a woman, -i / -e plural.
"To", in front of a place you are going: a Roma, a casa. The same little word comes back in M6 between andare and another verb — vado a mangiare. Neither job takes an article with a city name.

sentences.trap: English builds every past with "have" or with nothing. Italian picks the helper from the verb, and going is the commonest verb that picks essere — *ho andato is the mistake almost everyone makes once.
sentences.sound: an-DA-to. sono andato runs together with no break: so-no-an-DA-to.

variations.changed: -o → -a: the same sentence said by a woman, because essere makes the ending agree

variations.display: Ieri sono andato a casa presto
variations.changed: another destination, and the adverb still hugs the verb
sono → sei: the helper moves to you, and the participle keeps agreeing with you

mistake.why: andare takes essere: Ieri sono andato a Roma. avere is for nearly everything else.

sentences.usage: The other half of yesterday — not what you did, but where you went.
sentences.mnemonic: You GO with essere, and the ending goes with you.

words.note: The participle essere uses for its own past — and the participle of stare too, so sono stata covers both "I was" and "I stayed". The helper is essere, so the ending agrees: stato a man, stata a woman.

sentences.trap: essere's own past is built with essere: sono stato, sono stata. And since the helper is essere, the ending follows whoever is speaking — a man writing this sentence writes stato.
sentences.sound: STA-ta, stressed on the first syllable, both a's open and equal.

variations.changed: -a → -o: the same sentence said by a man
sono → sei: asked of a woman, so the participle stays feminine

variations.display: Ieri non sono stata a casa
variations.changed: non in front of the whole verb, helper and participle together

mistake.why: essere's own past takes essere: sono stata. And with essere the participle agrees — stata for a woman, stato for a man.

sentences.usage: Saying where you spent a day, or that you spent it nowhere at all.
sentences.mnemonic: essere goes back to itself: sono stato.

words.note: "What", asking about a thing — literally "what thing", and either half works alone: che hai mangiato? and cosa hai mangiato? are both said. Taught whole so the pair is learned as one question word.

sentences.trap: There is no "did" to front. The question phrase goes to the front, the two-word verb stays exactly as it was, and the question mark does the rest.
sentences.sound: ke-KO-za. che is KE — a c before h is always hard — and the single s between vowels is the one from casa.

variations.changed: swap the participle — the question phrase never changes
another participle behind the same helper
the answer: the helper swaps person and the question phrase drops away

mistake.why: The helper takes a PARTICIPLE, never the plain form: Che cosa hai mangiato ieri?

sentences.usage: The question that starts every conversation about a meal.
sentences.mnemonic: che cosa is "what thing" — and either word can carry it alone.

words.note: The participle of parlare (M4) — an -are verb, so -ato. Behind avere it is frozen: ho parlato whoever is speaking, and never ho parlata.

sentences.trap: With avere the participle is frozen. It moves only behind essere — so sono andata is right and ho parlata is not, even when a woman is speaking.
sentences.sound: par-LA-to, stressed in the middle, and the r is a single tap.

ho → hai, and a question mark rather than a fronted "did"

mistake.why: Behind avere the participle never moves: ho parlato, whoever is speaking. Agreement belongs to essere.

sentences.usage: Reporting a conversation without saying what was in it.
sentences.mnemonic: avere freezes the participle; essere lets it move.

words.note: The participle of studiare (M3) — an -are verb, so -ato. It rides avere, like every verb that acts on something.

sentences.trap: Both English pasts land on this one sentence: "I didn't study yesterday" and "I haven't studied yesterday" are the same Italian, and neither needs anything Italian has not already written.
sentences.sound: stu-DYA-to. The -dia- is one syllable, DYA, exactly as in studio.

variations.changed: drop non and the sentence turns positive
the participle takes its own object, and the negative is untouched
the helper moves to you and the negative drops away

mistake.why: studiare takes avere: ho studiato. Only the short essere list — andare, stare, essere and the reflexives — takes sono.

sentences.mnemonic: If the verb acts on something, it rides avere.

words.note: The participle of dormire, "to sleep" — the third verb class, so its ending is -ito. Sleeping acts on nothing, and it still takes avere: the essere list is a list, not a rule about what a verb means.

sentences.trap: -ire verbs take -ito, and that is the third and last of the participle endings. Learn the set — -ato, -uto, -ito — before meeting a single irregular one.
sentences.sound: dor-MI-to, stressed in the middle. The r is one tap and the final o is short.

ho → hai and a question mark — the morning's first question
swap the adverb — both bene and molto hug the verb

mistake.why: dormire is an -ire verb, so its participle is dormito. -uto belongs to the -ere class.
